To implement a custom permission, override
`BasePermission`
and implement either, or both, of the following methods:

`.has_permission(self, request, view)`
`.has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj)`

For example:


`defget_object(self):obj=get_object_or_404(self.get_queryset(),pk=self.kwargs["pk"])self.check_object_permissions(self.request,obj)returnobj`


Note
With the exception of
`DjangoObjectPermissions`
, the provided
permission classes in
`rest_framework.permissions`
do not
implement the
methods necessary to check object permissions.
If you wish to use the provided permission classes in order to check object

subclass them and implement the

#### Limitations of object level permissions¶ {#limitations-of-object-level-permissions}

For performance reasons the generic views will not automatically apply object level permissions to each instance in a queryset when returning a list of objects.

llm_response:
You should reach for a `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` when you want to provide only read-only operations for a model. You should use a `ModelViewSet` when you need to provide the full set of create, list, retrieve, update, and destroy actions.

The two classes differ in the following ways:

*   **Available Actions:** `ModelViewSet` provides the complete set of create, list, retrieve, update, and destroy actions by default. `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` only provides the 'read-only' actions: `.list()` and `.retrieve()`.
*   **Purpose:** `ModelViewSet` is used for viewing and editing instances, whereas `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` is used for viewing instances.

Both classes inherit from `GenericAPIView` and typically require you to provide the `queryset` and `serializer_class` attributes. If you need to restrict operations on a `ModelViewSet` to make it behave like a read-only view, you can use standard permission classes instead of switching to `ReadOnlyModelViewSet`.

`queryset`

`ViewSet`

`basename`
kwarg as part of your
router registration (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/routers/)
.

Also note that although this class provides the complete set of create/list/retrieve/update/destroy actions by default, you can restrict the available operations by using the standard permission classes.

Let's take our current set of views, and refactor them into view sets.

First of all let's refactor our
`UserList`
and
`UserDetail`
classes into a single
`UserViewSet`
class. In the
`snippets/views.py`
file, we can remove the two view classes and replace them with a single ViewSet class:


`fromrest_frameworkimportviewsetsclassUserViewSet(viewsets.ReadOnlyModelViewSet):"""This viewset automatically provides `list` and `retrieve` actions."""queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializer`


Here we've used the
`ReadOnlyModelViewSet`
class to automatically provide the default 'read-only' operations.  We're still setting the
`queryset`
and
`serializer_class`
attributes exactly as we did when we were using regular views, but we no longer need to provide the same information to two separate classes.

#### Example¶ {#example_1}

Because
`ModelViewSet`
extends
`GenericAPIView`
, you'll normally need to provide at least the
`queryset`
and
`serializer_class`
attributes.  For example:


`classAccountViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):"""
A simple ViewSet for viewing and editing accounts.
"""queryset=Account.objects.all()serializer_class=AccountSerializerpermission_classes=[IsAccountAdminOrReadOnly]`


Note that you can use any of the standard attributes or method overrides provided by
`GenericAPIView`
.  For example, to use a
`ViewSet`
that dynamically determines the queryset it should operate on, you might do something like this:

A simple ViewSet for viewing and editing the accounts
associated with the user.

`CustomReadOnlyRouter`
would generate for a simple viewset.

`views.py`
:

Returns a list of all the group names that the given
user belongs to.

`urls.py`
:


`router=CustomReadOnlyRouter()router.register('users',UserViewSet)urlpatterns=router.urls`

URL

For another example of setting the

Rather than writing your own viewsets, you'll often want to use the existing base classes that provide a default set of behavior.  For example:


`classUserViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):"""
A viewset for viewing and editing user instances.
"""serializer_class=UserSerializerqueryset=User.objects.all()`


There are two main advantages of using a
`ViewSet`
class over using a
`View`
class.

Repeated logic can be combined into a single class.  In the above example, we only need to specify the
`queryset`
once, and it'll be used across multiple views.
By using routers, we no longer need to deal with wiring up the URL conf ourselves.

Both of these come with a trade-off.  Using regular views and URL confs is more explicit and gives you more control.  ViewSets are helpful if you want to get up and running quickly, or when you have a large API and you want to enforce a consistent URL configuration throughout.

user_input: During tests I want to exercise my views like a client would — hitting URLs with get/post/put and JSON bodies — not building requests by hand. What does DRF give me?
reference: APIClient, which extends Django's test Client and supports the same .get()/.post()/.put()/.patch()/.delete()/.head()/.options() interface.
reference_contexts: The APIClient class supports the same request interface as Django's standard Client class.
This means that the standard .get() , .post() , .put() , .patch() , .delete() , .head() and .options() methods are all available.
llm_response:
To exercise your views like a client by hitting URLs with `get`, `post`, and `put` methods using JSON bodies, DRF provides the following options:

### 1. `APIClient` (Recommended)
The `APIClient` class extends Django's standard `Client` class and supports the same request interface, including `.get()`, `.post()`, `.put()`, `.patch()`, `.delete()`, `.head()`, and `.options()`. 

You can specify the format (e.g., `'json'`) directly in the request method:
```python
from rest_framework.test import APIClient
client = APIClient()
client.post('/notes/', {'title': 'new idea'}, format='json')
```
You can also set the default format for all test requests by adding the following to your `settings.py`:
```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'TEST_REQUEST_DEFAULT_FORMAT': 'json'
}
```

### 2. `RequestsClient`
For a more end-to-end testing experience that still runs entirely in-process against your local Django application, you can use `RequestsClient`. This allows you to interact with the API using URLs and JSON bodies as follows:
```python
client = RequestsClient()
response = client.post('http://testserver/organizations/', 
                       json={'name': 'MegaCorp', 'status': 'active'}, 
                       headers={'X-CSRFToken': csrftoken})
```

### Note on `APIRequestFactory`
While `APIRequestFactory` is available, it is used for testing views directly rather than hitting URLs. It requires you to manually call the view and render the response, and it does not provide the same client-like interface for hitting URLs as `APIClient` or `RequestsClient`.
llm_references:
For example...


`client=RequestsClient()# Obtain a CSRF token.response=client.get('http://testserver/homepage/')assertresponse.status_code==200csrftoken=response.cookies['csrftoken']# Interact with the API.response=client.post('http://testserver/organizations/',json={'name':'MegaCorp','status':'active'},headers={'X-CSRFToken':csrftoken})assertresponse.status_code==200`


### Live tests¶ {#live-tests}

With careful usage the
`RequestsClient`
provides the ability to write tests
that exercise your API views in a more end-to-end fashion than
`APIClient`
,
while still running entirely in-process against your local Django application.

This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

The simplest built-in scheme for quick testing with `curl` is **BasicAuthentication**. You can use it from the command line as shown in the following example:

`curl -u admin -H 'Accept: application/json; indent=4' http://127.0.0.1:8000/users/`

If you use `BasicAuthentication` in production, you must ensure the API is only available over `https`, that clients re-request credentials at login, and that credentials are never stored in persistent storage.

For later development, you should move off this to a more robust solution. The documentation suggests the following alternatives:

*   **TokenAuthentication**: A built-in, simple token-based scheme. If you require features like multiple tokens per user, tighter security, or token expiry, you should move to the third-party package **Django REST Knox**.
*   **JSON Web Token (JWT) Authentication**: A standard that does not require a database to validate tokens. The documentation recommends the third-party package **djangorestframework-simplejwt**.

user_input: When an unauthenticated request is rejected I sometimes get 401 and sometimes 403. What actually decides which one DRF returns?
reference: It hinges on whether the first/highest-priority authentication class uses a WWW-Authenticate header: if it does, an unauthenticated denial is 401 with that header; if not, it's 403. A request that authenticated but lacked permission is always 403.
reference_contexts: The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response .
The request was not successfully authenticated, and the highest priority authentication class does not use WWW-Authenticate headers.

Signature: AuthenticationFailed(detail=None, code=None) Raised when an incoming request includes incorrect authentication.
llm_response:
Whether DRF returns a 401 or 403 for an unauthenticated request depends on the following rules:

*   **403 Forbidden:** This is returned if the request was successfully authenticated but permission was denied, or if the highest priority authentication class does not use `WWW-Authenticate` headers.
*   **401 Unauthorized:** This is returned if the request was not successfully authenticated and the highest priority authentication class does use `WWW-Authenticate` headers.

**Determining the authentication scheme:**
*   The "highest priority" authentication class is the first authentication class set on the view.
*   If an authentication scheme does not override the `.authenticate_header()` method, it will return a 403 Forbidden response when an unauthenticated request is denied access.
*   If the `.authenticate_header()` method is implemented, it returns a string used as the value of the `WWW-Authenticate` header, resulting in a 401 Unauthorized response.

**Exceptions:**
*   If a request is successfully authenticated but denied permission, a 403 Forbidden response is always used, regardless of the authentication scheme.
*   Specific authentication schemes, such as `SessionAuthentication`, are documented to result in a 403 Forbidden response for unauthenticated requests that are denied permission.

user_input: The OpenAPI file we publish is missing a good chunk of the API. None of the custom actions we hung off our viewsets appear in it at all, and several endpoints that do appear describe their request body as empty even though they clearly accept one. Nothing fails — the generate step exits cleanly and writes the file. What is actually walking the project to build this, where does the per-endpoint detail come from, and why would an endpoint come out blank rather than wrong?
reference: Schema generation is two layers, and your two symptoms come from different ones. SchemaGenerator is the top-level piece: it walks your configured URL patterns, finds the APIView subclasses behind them, asks each one for its schema representation, and compiles the result — so anything not reachable through the URL conf simply isn't seen, which is the first thing to check for the missing actions. The per-view detail comes from AutoSchema, which is attached to each view through its `schema` attribute and does the introspection; you subclass AutoSchema to customise what a view reports, and set a project-wide default with the DEFAULT_SCHEMA_CLASS setting. An endpoint comes out blank rather than wrong when the introspection has nothing to infer from — there's no serializer for it to read — which is why the docs tell you to annotate the generated schema with any additional information that cannot be automatically inferred. Worth knowing before you invest in this: the built-in schema support is deprecated in favour of third-party packages, and drf-spectacular is the recommended full replacement.
reference_contexts: SchemaGenerator is a top-level class that is responsible for walking your configured URL patterns, finding APIView subclasses, enquiring for their schema representation, and compiling the final schema object.
AutoSchema encapsulates all the details necessary for per-view schema introspection. Is attached to each view via the schema attribute. You subclass AutoSchema in order to customize your schema.
settings.DEFAULT_SCHEMA_CLASS allows you to specify an AutoSchema subclass to serve as your project's default.
Once you've generated a schema in this way you can annotate it with any additional information that cannot be automatically inferred by the schema generator.

REST framework's built-in support for generating OpenAPI schemas is deprecated in favor of 3rd party packages that can provide this functionality instead. As a full-fledged replacement, we recommend the drf-spectacular package.
llm_response:
The `SchemaGenerator` class is responsible for walking your configured URL patterns, identifying `APIView` subclasses, and compiling the final schema object [6].

Per-endpoint detail is handled by the `AutoSchema` class, which is attached to each view via the `schema` attribute and encapsulates the details necessary for view introspection [6]. Specifically, `get_operation()` is the main entry point for this introspection, returning the OpenAPI operation object that describes the endpoint [1].

Regarding why endpoints appear blank or missing:
*   **Missing custom actions:** The `SchemaGenerator` walks your configured URL patterns to find `APIView` subclasses [6]. If your custom actions are not being picked up, ensure they are correctly routed within your URL patterns [5].
*   **Blank request bodies:** The `AutoSchema` class is responsible for the introspection of these details [6]. If an endpoint appears with an empty request body, it is because the `AutoSchema` (or the subclass you have implemented) is not correctly identifying or mapping the request body during the introspection process [1, 6]. 

To customize or fix how these details are generated, you should subclass `AutoSchema` and override methods like `get_operation()` or `map_field()` [1, 6]. You can set your custom class as the project default using `settings.DEFAULT_SCHEMA_CLASS` [6].

user_input: I'm weighing limiting a queryset vs permission classes vs the serializer to restrict access. What can each control, especially for list vs create?
reference: queryset/get_queryset limits which existing objects are visible globally; permission_classes do action/object-level checks but object-level only applies to retrieve/modify/delete; serializer_class restricts at instance level on input/output. Object-level checks don't run on create because get_object isn't called.
reference_contexts: REST framework offers three different methods to customize access restrictions on a case-by-case basis.
These apply in different scenarios and have different effects and limitations.
Because the get_object() method is not called, object level permissions from the has_object_permission() method are not applied when creating objects.
The simplest way to filter the queryset of any view that subclasses GenericAPIView is to override the .get_queryset() method.
The ModelSerializer class provides a shortcut that lets you automatically create a Serializer class with fields that correspond to the Model fields.
llm_response:
The three methods offer different levels of control for `list` and `create` actions:

### **1. Queryset (`queryset` / `get_queryset()`)**
*   **List:** Provides **global** control. It limits the general visibility of objects from the database. You should use this to ensure users only have visibility onto instances they are permitted to view. By overriding `get_queryset()`, you can filter results based on the current user or URL parameters.
*   **Create:** Offers **no** control over the creation action.

### **2. Permission Classes (`permission_classes` / `get_permissions()`)**
*   **List:** Provides **global** control. Checks are applied to the entire object type, subject to the restrictions already applied by the queryset.
*   **Create:** Provides **global** control. Because `get_object()` is not called during creation, object-level permissions (`has_object_permission()`) are not applied. To restrict creation, you must implement the check in your serializer or override the `perform_create()` method in your ViewSet.

### **3. Serializer (`serializer_class` / `get_serializer()`)**
*   **List:** Provides **object-level** control. However, you should not raise `PermissionDenied` here, as it would prevent the entire list from being returned.
*   **Create:** Provides **object-level** control. This is one of the recommended places to implement permission checks for object creation.

### **Summary Table**

| Method | List Action | Create Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Queryset** | Global | No |
| **Permission Classes** | Global | Global |
| **Serializer** | Object-level* | Object-level |

*\*Note: A Serializer should not raise `PermissionDenied` in a list action.*

**Decision-making capabilities:**
*   **`get_*()` methods:** By overriding `get_queryset()`, `get_permissions()`, or `get_serializer()`, you can access the current view and return different instances based on the **request** or **action**.
*   **Permission Classes:** Can reference the **action** and the **request** in their decision-making.
*   **Serializer:** Can reference the **request** via the context.

llm_response:
To build your snippets API with automatic URL routing and the required ownership permissions, you should wire together the following DRF components:

### 1. ViewSet
Use a `viewsets.ModelViewSet` to group your snippet logic into a single class. This provides the `list`, `create`, `retrieve`, `update`, and `destroy` actions automatically. 
*   **Permissions:** Define `permission_classes` within the `SnippetViewSet` to enforce your requirements. Use `permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly` combined with a custom `IsOwnerOrReadOnly` class to ensure only the owner can edit or delete.
*   **Ownership:** Override the `perform_create` method in your `SnippetViewSet` to save the owner automatically:
    ```python
    def perform_create(self, serializer):
        serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
    ```

### 2. Serializer
Use a `serializers.ModelSerializer` (or `HyperlinkedModelSerializer`) to define the API representation of your snippet model. Ensure the serializer includes the owner field so that the relationship is handled correctly.

### 3. Router
To avoid hand-writing `urls.py` entries, use the `DefaultRouter` class. This is the recommended approach for handling URL configuration when using `ViewSets`.

**How to wire them together:**
1.  **Register the ViewSet:** In your `urls.py`, instantiate the `DefaultRouter` and register your `SnippetViewSet`.
    ```python
    from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
    from snippets import views

    router = DefaultRouter()
    router.register(r"snippets", views.SnippetViewSet, basename="snippet")
    ```
2.  **Include in URL patterns:** Add the router's generated URLs to your `urlpatterns`.
    ```python
    urlpatterns = [
        path("", include(router.urls)),
    ]
    ```

Using the `DefaultRouter` automatically generates the URL configuration for your API, including the API root view, and avoids the need to manually define paths for each list or detail route.

reference: DRF's reverse ties into the versioning scheme, so pass the current request as a keyword argument; reverse then applies the URL transformations for that request's version and returns a fully qualified URL from the request's host/port.

llm_response:
The `reverse()` function ties into the versioning scheme to ensure that generated URLs match the version of the incoming request. To ensure the correct version is used, you must pass the current `request` object as a keyword argument to the function:

```python
from rest_framework.reverse import reverse
reverse('bookings-list', request=request)
```

When this is provided, the function applies the appropriate URL transformations based on the versioning scheme in use (e.g., prepending a namespace for `NamespaceVersioning` or adding a query parameter for `QueryParameterVersioning`). 

Additionally, if you are using hyperlinked serialization styles with a URL-based versioning scheme, you must include the request as context to the serializer to ensure relationships resolve to the same API version as the incoming request.

user_input: I want per-view control over both the authentication scheme and the permissions on one endpoint. How do these relate and how do I set both on one APIView?
reference: They're separate but sequential: authentication identifies the request and runs first (setting request.user/request.auth), then permissions use that to allow or deny. Set authentication_classes and permission_classes together — authentication alone never grants access.
reference_contexts: Note Don't forget that authentication by itself won't allow or disallow an incoming request , it simply identifies the credentials that the request was made with.
Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the request.user and request.auth properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.
— Apple Developer Documentation Together with authentication and throttling , permissions determine whether a request should be granted or denied access.
HTTP/1.1 420 Enhance Your Calm Twitter API rate limiting response Throttling is similar to permissions , in that it determines if a request should be authorized.
llm_response:
To set per-view control over both the authentication scheme and permissions on an `APIView`, you define the `authentication_classes` and `permission_classes` attributes directly on your class-based view. Setting these attributes tells the view to ignore the default lists defined in your `settings.py` file.

You can implement both on one `APIView` as follows:

```python
from rest_framework.authentication import SessionAuthentication, BasicAuthentication
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class ExampleView(APIView):
    authentication_classes = [SessionAuthentication, BasicAuthentication]
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get(self, request, format=None):
        content = {'status': 'request was permitted'}
        return Response(content)
```

Regarding how they relate: the `APIView` class ensures that the `.authenticators` property is automatically set based on the `authentication_classes` you provide. When you apply these settings, the authentication scheme determines the identity of the user (or `None`), and the permission policy then uses that information to determine whether to allow or deny access to the endpoint.

user_input: When I POST invalid data, where does the flow that turns a serializer error into a 400 actually come from — the serializer or the view?
reference: Both cooperate: the serializer's is_valid(raise_exception=True) raises ValidationError, the generic views use raise_exception=True, and DRF's default exception handler converts it to a 400.
reference_contexts: The .is_valid() method takes an optional raise_exception flag that will cause it to raise a serializers.ValidationError exception if there are validation errors.
is_valid ( raise_exception = True ) The generic views use the raise_exception=True flag, which means that you can override the style of validation error responses globally in your API.
By default this exception results in a response with the HTTP status code "400 Bad Request".
llm_response:
The flow that turns a serializer error into a 400 response depends on how the view is implemented:

*   **Manual handling in the view:** In basic views (such as those using the `@api_view` decorator), the view itself is responsible for checking `serializer.is_valid()` and explicitly returning a response with a 400 status code using `serializer.errors` [1, 2].
*   **Automatic handling via `raise_exception=True`:** If you call `serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)`, the serializer raises a `serializers.ValidationError` exception [3, 4]. This exception is then automatically caught by the REST framework's default exception handler, which returns an `HTTP 400 Bad Request` response [4]. Generic views use this flag by default [3].

Additionally, if the 400 error is caused by malformed content rather than serializer validation, the `APIView` class or `@api_view` decorator catches the resulting `ParseError` and returns a 400 response automatically [6].

To inject the current user and perform additional validation right before the database write in a generic view, you should use the `perform_create(self, serializer)` hook (for creation) or the `perform_update(self, serializer)` hook (for updates).

**Implementation:**
You can perform the validation and save the object by calling `serializer.save()` with the user attribute within these methods. For example:

```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):

    if some_condition:

    serializer.save(user=self.request.user)
```

When you raise a `ValidationError` within these hooks, it is handled by the REST framework's default exception handler. By default, this results in a response with an HTTP 400 Bad Request status code. You can customize the style of these error responses globally by using the `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` settings key.

### How hyperlinked views are determined¶ {#how-hyperlinked-views-are-determined}

There needs to be a way of determining which views should be used for hyperlinking to model instances.

By default hyperlinks are expected to correspond to a view name that matches the style
`'{model_name}-detail'`
, and looks up the instance by a
`pk`
keyword argument.

You can override a URL field view name and lookup field by using either, or both of, the
`view_name`
and
`lookup_field`
options in the
`extra_kwargs`
setting, like so:


`classAccountSerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):classMeta:model=Accountfields=['url','account_name','users','created']extra_kwargs={'url':{'view_name':'accounts','lookup_field':'account_name'},'users':{'lookup_field':'username'}}`


Alternatively you can set the fields on the serializer explicitly. For example:

You can explicitly include the primary key by adding it to the
`fields`
option, for example:


`classAccountSerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):classMeta:model=Accountfields=['url','id','account_name','users','created']`


### Absolute and relative URLs¶ {#absolute-and-relative-urls}

When instantiating a
`HyperlinkedModelSerializer`
you must include the current
`request`
in the serializer context, for example:


`serializer=AccountSerializer(queryset,context={'request':request})`


Doing so will ensure that the hyperlinks can include an appropriate hostname,
so that the resulting representation uses fully qualified URLs, such as:


`http://api.example.com/accounts/1/`


Rather than relative URLs, such as:


`/accounts/1/`


If you
do
want to use relative URLs, you should explicitly pass
`{'request': None}`
in the serializer context.

Alternatively you can set the fields on the serializer explicitly. For example:


`classAccountSerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):url=serializers.HyperlinkedIdentityField(view_name='accounts',lookup_field='slug')users=serializers.HyperlinkedRelatedField(view_name='user-detail',lookup_field='username',many=True,read_only=True)classMeta:model=Accountfields=['url','account_name','users','created']`

user_input: Our album list endpoint went from 40ms to about four seconds after I changed the tracks field to render the full nested track objects instead of just their ids. Someone told me to add select_related('tracks') to the queryset and the ORM threw an error at me instead. Why doesn't the framework deal with this itself, and how do I tell which optimisation goes with which field?
reference: The framework deliberately doesn't optimise the queryset for you — it makes no attempt to infer select_related / prefetch_related from your serializer, because that would be too much magic. Any field that spans an ORM relation, whether it's a declared relational field or a plain field reaching across a relation via `source`, can cost an extra query per object, and with many=True over a large queryset that becomes the N+1 you're seeing. Fixing it is your job, and which tool applies is decided by the relation, not by the serializer: select_related resolves forward single-valued relations (ForeignKey, OneToOne) with a SQL join, while a reverse or multi-valued relation like `tracks` cannot be joined that way and has to use prefetch_related — which is exactly why select_related('tracks') errored. Pass the optimised queryset to the serializer (Album.objects.prefetch_related('tracks')) and the extra hits disappear.
reference_contexts: REST Framework does not attempt to automatically optimize querysets passed to serializers in terms of select_related and prefetch_related since it would be too much magic. A serializer with a field spanning an ORM relation through its source attribute could require an additional database hit to fetch related objects from the database. It is the programmer's responsibility to optimize queries to avoid additional database hits which could occur while using a serializer.
If AlbumSerializer is used to serialize a fairly large queryset with many=True then it could be a serious performance problem.
qs = Album.objects.prefetch_related('tracks') # No additional database hits required print(AlbumSerializer(qs, many=True).data)
llm_response:
REST Framework does not automatically optimize querysets because it would be "too much magic." It is the programmer's responsibility to optimize queries to avoid the additional database hits that occur when a serializer spans an ORM relation.

The error you encountered likely occurred because you used `select_related()` for a relationship that requires `prefetch_related()`. You can determine which method to use based on the type of relationship:

*   **`select_related()`**: Use this for `ForeignKey` and `OneToOneField` relationships. It fetches the related object in the same database query.
*   **`prefetch_related()`**: Use this for reverse relationships and many-to-many relationships. It loads collections of related objects efficiently.

Since your `Album` model has a `ForeignKey` from `Track` to `Album` with a `related_name='tracks'`, the `tracks` field represents a reverse relationship. Therefore, you must use `prefetch_related('tracks')` in your queryset rather than `select_related('tracks')`.

You can apply this optimization by overriding the `get_queryset()` method in your view or by setting the `queryset` attribute on your view class:

```python
def get_queryset(self):
    return Album.objects.prefetch_related("tracks")
```

Note
REST Framework does not attempt to automatically optimize querysets passed to serializers in terms of
`select_related`
and
`prefetch_related`
since it would be too much magic. A serializer with a field spanning an ORM relation through its source attribute could require an additional database hit to fetch related objects from the database. It is the programmer's responsibility to optimize queries to avoid additional database hits which could occur while using such a serializer.
For example, the following serializer would lead to a database hit each time evaluating the tracks field if it is not prefetched:

`classAlbumSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):tracks=serializers.SlugRelatedField(many=True,read_only=True,slug_field='title')classMeta:model=Albumfields=['album_name','artist','tracks']# For each album object, tracks should be fetched from databaseqs=Album.objects.all()print(AlbumSerializer(qs,many=True).data)`

`prefetch_related()`

llm_response:
To automatically generate an auth token for every user at account creation, use the `post_save` signal. Place the following code in an installed `models.py` module or another location imported by Django on startup:

```python
from django.conf import settings
from django.db.models.signals import post_save
from django.dispatch import receiver
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

@receiver(post_save, sender=settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL)
def create_auth_token(sender, instance=None, created=False, **kwargs):
    if created:
        Token.objects.create(user=instance)
```

To backfill tokens for existing users, run the following code:

```python
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

for user in User.objects.all():
    Token.objects.get_or_create(user=user)
```

reference: request.data is DRF's flexible replacement for request.POST: it handles arbitrary parsed content for POST, PUT and PATCH, not just form data. The parser classes DRF selects do the actual parsing, so request.data works across formats like JSON.
reference_contexts: The core functionality of the Request object is the request.data attribute, which is similar to request.POST , but more useful for working with Web APIs.
request.data can handle incoming json requests, but it can also handle other formats.

The wrappers also provide behavior such as returning 405 Method Not Allowed responses when appropriate, and handling any ParseError exceptions that occur when accessing request.data with malformed input.
request.data will be populated with a dictionary of data.
request.query_params is a more correctly named synonym for request.GET .
llm_response:
DRF's `Request` object provides flexible request parsing that allows you to access the parsed content of the request body via the `request.data` attribute. When you access `request.data`, REST framework examines the `Content-Type` header of the incoming request to determine which parser class to use to parse the content. You can define the valid parsers for a view by setting a list of classes in the `parser_classes` attribute (for `APIView`) or using the `@parser_classes` decorator (for function-based views).

Compared to `request.POST`, `request.data` provides the following advantages:

*   **Arbitrary Data Support:** It supports REST framework's flexible parsing, allowing you to handle media types like JSON in addition to form data.
*   **Method Support:** It works for `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` methods, whereas `request.POST` only works for `POST` requests.
*   **Comprehensive Content:** It includes all parsed content, covering both file and non-file inputs.

The `DefaultRouter` class automatically creates the API root view for you, so you can delete your hand-written `api_root` function.

Regarding how registrations map to URLs:

*   **Automatic Generation:** When you register a ViewSet with a router, the router automatically determines the URL configuration. You provide two arguments to the `register` method: the URL prefix for the views and the ViewSet itself.
*   **URL Inclusion:** You can include the router's generated URLs in your `urlpatterns` using `path("", include(router.urls))`.
*   **Prefixing:** When registering, do not include a trailing slash in the prefix (e.g., use `r'users'`, not `r'users/'`). The router appends slashes automatically based on your configuration.
*   **Basename:** If the router cannot automatically determine the `basename` from the model name, you must explicitly set the `basename` argument when registering the ViewSet.
*   **Flexibility:** The `router.urls` attribute is a standard list of URL patterns. You can append these to existing lists of views or use them with Django's `include` function.

user_input: I swapped in a cut-down metadata class so OPTIONS stops advertising our whole field list to anonymous clients. Now the front-end team reports that their OPTIONS call comes back as an HTML page while mine comes back as JSON — same endpoint, same deploy, and neither of us touched the renderer config. What decides what goes into that response versus what format it arrives in?
reference: Two separate mechanisms compose on that one response, which is why changing one didn't explain the other. The metadata class decides the *content* of an OPTIONS body: DEFAULT_METADATA_CLASS (or a per-view `metadata_class`) names a class implementing determine_metadata(request, view), and the built-in SimpleMetadata is what returns the name, description, renders/parses lists and the `actions` field descriptions — a MinimalMetadata-style override returning just name and description is what trimmed it. The *format* is then chosen by content negotiation, which picks a renderer from the ones configured for the view based on the client's Accept header, most specific first, falling back to the order of renderer_classes / DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES when specificity ties. A browser sends Accept: text/html and gets the browsable renderer; a fetch() sending Accept: application/json gets JSON. Same metadata payload, two representations.
reference_contexts: REST framework includes a configurable mechanism for determining how your API should respond to OPTIONS requests. This allows you to return API schema or other resource information.
If you want to provide a custom metadata class you should override BaseMetadata and implement the determine_metadata(self, request, view) method.

REST framework uses a simple style of content negotiation to determine which media type should be returned to a client, based on the available renderers, the priorities of each of those renderers, and the client's Accept: header. The style used is partly client-driven, and partly server-driven.
If multiple media types have the same specificity, then preference is given to based on the ordering of the renderers configured for the given view.
llm_response:
The format of the `OPTIONS` response is determined by the content negotiation stage, which uses the client's `Accept` header to select the appropriate renderer.

*   **What decides the format:** The response format is determined by the negotiated renderer, which is selected based on the client's `Accept` header. The system uses the highest priority renderer available, excluding `BrowsableAPIRenderer` by default.
*   **What decides the content:** The content of the `OPTIONS` response is determined by the `metadata_class` assigned to the view (or the global `DEFAULT_METADATA_CLASS`). The `determine_metadata(self, request, view)` method of that class generates the data that is subsequently rendered into the format chosen during content negotiation.

Because the front-end team and you are receiving different formats from the same endpoint, it indicates that your respective clients are sending different `Accept` headers, causing the content negotiation process to select different renderers (e.g., `JSONRenderer` versus an HTML-based renderer).

To use `DjangoModelPermissions`, your view must expose either a `.queryset` property or a `.get_queryset()` method. The permission class determines the appropriate model by checking `queryset.model` or `get_queryset().model`.

*   **PUT** and **PATCH**: Require the `change` permission.
*   **DELETE**: Requires the `delete` permission.

Signature:

### NotFound¶ {#notfound}

### MethodNotAllowed¶ {#methodnotallowed}

Signature:
`MethodNotAllowed(method, detail=None, code=None)`

Raised when an incoming request occurs that does not map to a handler method on the view.

By default this exception results in a response with the HTTP status code "405 Method Not Allowed".

`NotAcceptable(detail=None, code=None)`

reference: For reads, nested relationships are expressed by using serializers as fields (add many=True for to-many). Writing isn't automatic: because nested creates/updates are ambiguous, REST framework 3 requires you to write .create()/.update() explicitly.
reference_contexts: Such nested relationships can be expressed by using serializers as fields.
If the field is used to represent a to-many relationship, you should add the many=True flag to the serializer field.

save () return instance Because the behavior of nested creates and updates can be ambiguous, and may require complex dependencies between related models, REST framework 3 requires you to always write these methods explicitly.
llm_response:
For reads, DRF automatically handles nested representations, and the `.validated_data` property will include nested data structures.

For writes, DRF does not support writable nested representations by default. The default `ModelSerializer` `.create()` and `.update()` methods do not include this support, and you must write these methods explicitly to handle saving multiple related objects.

Alternatively, you can use third-party packages such as **DRF Writable Nested** to support automatic writable nested representations, or write custom model manager classes to handle creating the correct instances.

user_input: I added our logo to the browsable API by dropping in my own template, and after that deploy the login/logout control disappeared from the navbar. The auth routes are still in the urlconf and I never touched them. How do the template customisation and the login control relate — what do I have to preserve so both survive?
reference: They meet in the same template. The login control only appears if you've routed it — you add the 'login' and 'logout' routes under the 'rest_framework' namespace by including rest_framework.urls in your urlconf — but it is *rendered* by rest_framework/base.html. Customisation is supposed to be additive: you create rest_framework/api.html that `{% extends "rest_framework/base.html" %}` and override individual blocks (bootstrap_theme to swap the Bootstrap CSS, bootstrap_navbar_variant for the navbar style, style for finer CSS tweaks). If your api.html replaces base.html's content instead of extending it and overriding a block, you drop everything base.html was rendering — the auth control included — even though the routes are still registered. Extend, override the one block you need, and the login link comes back.

If you open a browser and navigate to the browsable API at the moment, you'll find that you're no longer able to create new code snippets.  In order to do so we'd need to be able to login as a user.

`urls.py`

user_input: The same serializer renders correct absolute links when it's driven by our list view, but when a nightly management command instantiates it directly to build a digest email, the link fields blow up. Nothing about the serializer differs between the two paths. What is the view handing the serializer that my command isn't, and how do I supply it myself?
reference: The view is passing serializer context, and the hyperlinked fields depend on it. Fully qualified URLs can't be built from the model alone — the serializer needs the current request to know the scheme and host — so hyperlinked relations require the request to be in context. Generic views do this for you when they instantiate the serializer, which is why the list endpoint works and your standalone call doesn't. Outside a view you pass it yourself: AccountSerializer(queryset, many=True, context={'request': request}). Context is the general mechanism for handing a serializer anything beyond the object being serialized, and it's readable as self.context from any field logic such as a custom to_representation(). If you genuinely want relative URLs — plausible for an email — you must pass {'request': None} explicitly rather than omitting the key.
reference_contexts: There are some cases where you need to provide extra context to the serializer in addition to the object being serialized. One common case is if you're using a serializer that includes hyperlinked relations, which requires the serializer to have access to the current request so that it can properly generate fully qualified URLs.
You can provide arbitrary additional context by passing a context argument when instantiating the serializer.
The context dictionary can be used within any serializer field logic, such as a custom .to_representation() method, by accessing the self.context attribute.
When instantiating a HyperlinkedModelSerializer you must include the current request in the serializer context, for example: serializer = AccountSerializer(queryset, context={'request': request})
If you do want to use relative URLs, you should explicitly pass {'request': None} in the serializer context.
llm_response:
The view is providing a `request` object in the serializer's context, which is required for the serializer to build absolute URLs. When you manually instantiate a serializer, you must explicitly pass this context.

To fix this in your management command, update your instantiation to include the `request` object:

`serializer = YourSerializer(instance, context={'request': request})`

If you do not have a request object available in your management command and wish to use relative URLs instead, you should pass `{'request': None}` in the context.

What was producing that per-field structure before, and what do I have to keep in my own handler to get it back?
reference: The per-field structure came from the default exception handler, and you replaced it. The chain is: generic views call is_valid(raise_exception=True), which turns a failed validation into a raised ValidationError; the framework's exception handler catches that and renders it as the field-keyed 400 body your front-end was parsing. Your custom handler is wired in through the EXCEPTION_HANDLER setting and takes (exc, context), and it must either return a Response or return None to re-raise — returning your own freshly built Response discards that rendering. The documented pattern is to call REST framework's own exception_handler first to get the standard error response, then decorate what it returned (e.g. adding to response.data) rather than constructing a replacement. Because generic views use raise_exception=True, fixing the handler this way changes validation error style globally across the API.
reference_contexts: The function must take a pair of arguments, the first is the exception to be handled, and the second is a dictionary containing any extra context such as the view currently being handled. The exception handler function should either return a Response object, or return None if the exception cannot be handled.

from rest_framework.views import exception_handler def custom_exception_handler(exc, context): # Call REST framework's default exception handler first, to get the standard error response. response = exception_handler(exc, context)
The exception handler must also be configured in your settings, using the EXCEPTION_HANDLER setting key.
The generic views use the raise_exception=True flag, which means that you can override the style of validation error responses globally in your API. To do so, use a custom exception handler.

When a `ValidationError` occurs, the error object contains the field names as keys (or the `NON_FIELD_ERRORS_KEY` for non-field-specific errors) [4]. You must include these keys in the response body of your handler rather than flattening the error details into a single string [4, 6].

## Custom exception handling¶ {#custom-exception-handling}

You can implement custom exception handling by creating a handler function that converts exceptions raised in your API views into response objects.  This allows you to control the style of error responses used by your API.

The function must take a pair of arguments, the first is the exception to be handled, and the second is a dictionary containing any extra context such as the view currently being handled. The exception handler function should either return a
`Response`
object, or return
`None`
if the exception cannot be handled.  If the handler returns
`None`
then the exception will be re-raised and Django will return a standard HTTP 500 'server error' response.

Both styles "
`PUT`
as 404" and "
`PUT`
as create" can be valid in different circumstances, but we've now opted for the 404 behavior as the default, due to it being simpler and more obvious.

If you need to restore the previous behavior you may want to include
this AllowPUTAsCreateMixin class (https://gist.github.com/tomchristie/a2ace4577eff2c603b1b)
as a mixin to your views.

#### Customizing error responses.¶ {#customizing-error-responses}

The generic views now raise
`ValidationFailed`
exception for invalid data. This exception is then dealt with by the exception handler, rather than the view returning a
`400 Bad Request`
response directly.

This change means that you can now easily customize the style of error responses across your entire API, without having to modify any of the generic views.

To implement custom authentication, you should override the `.authenticate(self, request)` method. The behavior depends on whether authentication is attempted or not:

*   **If authentication is not attempted:** Return `None`. This allows other authentication schemes in the list to be checked.
*   **If authentication is attempted but fails:** Raise an `AuthenticationFailed` exception. This causes an error response to be returned immediately, bypassing any further authentication schemes and permission checks.

When an authentication scheme fails, you may optionally override the `.authenticate_header(self, request)` method to return a string used for the `WWW-Authenticate` header in a `HTTP 401 Unauthorized` response. If this method is not overridden, the scheme will return `HTTP 403 Forbidden` responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

To implement a custom authentication scheme, subclass

`(user, auth)`
if authentication succeeds, or
`None`
otherwise.

In some circumstances instead of returning
`None`

`AuthenticationFailed`
exception from the
`.authenticate()`
method.

If the
`.authenticate_header()`
method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will return
`HTTP 403 Forbidden`
responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

Note
When your custom authenticator is invoked by the request object's
`.user`
or
`.auth`
properties, you may see an
`AttributeError`
re-raised as a
`WrappedAttributeError`

`AttributeError`
originates from your custom authenticator and will instead assume that the request object does not have a
`.user`
or
`.auth`
property. These errors should be fixed or otherwise handled by your authenticator.

## How authentication is determined¶ {#how-authentication-is-determined}

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,
`request.user`
will be set to an instance of
`django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser`
, and
`request.auth`
will be set to
`None`
.

The value of
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
for unauthenticated requests can be modified using the
`UNAUTHENTICATED_USER`
and
`UNAUTHENTICATED_TOKEN`
settings.

## Setting the authentication scheme¶ {#setting-the-authentication-scheme}

The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`

`CursorPagination` rules out deep-linking to specific pages because it only provides forward and reverse controls and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions [1].

Regarding the data underneath, `CursorPagination` requires a unique, unchanging ordering of items [1]. Specifically, the ordering field must satisfy the following:

*   **Unchanging:** It must be a value set only once, such as a creation timestamp or slug [5].
*   **Unique or nearly unique:** While it supports not-strictly-unique values via a "position plus offset" style, it is best used with unique values like millisecond-precision timestamps [5].
*   **Non-nullable:** It must be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string [5].
*   **Data type:** It should not be a float, as precision errors can lead to incorrect results; decimals are recommended instead [5].
*   **Database index:** The field used for ordering should have a database index [5].

### CursorPagination¶ {#cursorpagination}

The cursor-based pagination presents an opaque "cursor" indicator that the client may use to page through the result set. This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail. You'll need to think about what ordering you want the scheme to be applied against. The default is to order by
`"-created"`
. This assumes that
there must be a 'created' timestamp field
on the model instances, and will present a "timeline" style paginated view, with the most recently added items first.

Using an ordering field that does not satisfy these constraints will generally still work, but you'll be losing some of the benefits of cursor pagination.

For more technical details on the implementation we use for cursor pagination, the
"Building cursors for the Disqus API" (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
blog post gives a good overview of the basic approach.

#### Setup¶ {#setup_2}

To enable the
`CursorPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration, modifying the
`PAGE_SIZE`
as desired:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.CursorPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`


On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`CursorPagination`
on a per-view basis.

#### Configuration¶ {#configuration_2}

The
`CursorPagination`
class includes a number of attributes that may be overridden to modify the pagination style.

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. Much credit goes to David Cramer for
this blog post (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
on the subject.

#### Pagination controls in the browsable API.¶ {#pagination-controls-in-the-browsable-api}

Paginated results now include controls that render directly in the browsable API. If you're using the page or limit/offset style, then you'll see a page based control displayed in the browsable API:

Proper usage of cursor pagination should have an ordering field that satisfies the following:

Should be an unchanging value, such as a timestamp, slug, or other field that is only set once, on creation.
Should be unique, or nearly unique. Millisecond precision timestamps are a good example. This implementation of cursor pagination uses a smart "position plus offset" style that allows it to properly support not-strictly-unique values as the ordering.
Should be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string.
Should not be a float. Precision errors easily lead to incorrect results.
Hint: use decimals instead.
(If you already have a float field and must paginate on that, an
example CursorPagination subclass that uses decimals to limit precision is available here (https://gist.github.com/keturn/8bc88525a183fd41c73ffb729b8865be#file-fpcursorpagination-py)
.)
The field should have a database index.

# Pagination - Django REST framework

# Pagination¶ {#pagination}

Django provides a few classes that help you manage paginated data – that is, data that’s split across several pages, with “Previous/Next” links.
—
Django documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/pagination/)

REST framework includes support for customizable pagination styles. This allows you to modify how large result sets are split into individual pages of data.

The pagination API can support either:

Pagination links that are provided as part of the content of the response.
Pagination links that are included in response headers, such as
`Content-Range`
or
`Link`
.

The built-in styles currently all use links included as part of the content of the response. This style is more accessible when using the browsable API.

Paginated results now include controls that render directly in the browsable API. If you're using the page or limit/offset style, then you'll see a page based control displayed in the browsable API:

The cursor based pagination renders a more simple style of control:

#### Support for header-based pagination.¶ {#support-for-header-based-pagination}

The pagination API was previously only able to alter the pagination style in the body of the response. The API now supports being able to write pagination information in response headers, making it possible to use pagination schemes that use the
`Link`
or
`Content-Range`
headers.

For more information, see the
custom pagination styles (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/pagination/#custom-pagination-styles)
documentation.

llm_response:
The throttle count is stored in Django's cache framework. Because you are using local in-process caches (`LocMemCache`) on each of your three servers, each server maintains its own independent count, which explains why your client is able to exceed the 100/day limit by hitting different servers.

To move the count to a location all three servers can see, you must configure a shared cache backend in your Django settings (such as Redis or Memcached) instead of the default `LocMemCache`. 

Once a shared cache is configured in your Django `CACHES` setting, the built-in throttle classes will automatically use it if it is set as the `'default'` cache. If you need to use a specific shared cache that is not the `'default'`, you must create a custom throttle class and set its `cache` attribute:

```python
from django.core.cache import caches
from rest_framework.throttling import AnonRateThrottle # or UserRateThrottle, etc.

class CustomRateThrottle(AnonRateThrottle):
    cache = caches['your_shared_cache_name']
```

After creating the custom class, you must register it by updating your `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` setting or by using the `throttle_classes` view attribute.

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

The built-in throttle implementations are open to
race conditions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_condition#Data_race)
, so under high concurrency they may allow a few extra requests through.

If your project relies on guaranteeing the number of requests during concurrent requests, you will need to implement your own throttle class. See
issue #5181 (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/issues/5181)
for more details.

The application-level throttling provided by REST framework is intended for implementing policies such as different business tiers and basic protections against service over-use.

reference: Two knobs, and the URL one is itself two values. The router picks up methods decorated with @action and generates routes for them, with `detail=True` or `detail=False` deciding whether the pattern carries a pk. By default the URL pattern comes from the method name and the URL *name* is the viewset's basename joined to the hyphenated method name — and `url_path` and `url_name` change those two independently. Changing only url_path leaves the reverse name as it was, so a serializer reversing the name you assumed gets NoReverseMatch; set both, or reverse the name that's actually registered. Permissions are separate: @action accepts `permission_classes`, e.g. @action(detail=True, methods=['post'], permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf]). Two things stop those from firing. Object-level checks only run when the object is fetched through get_object(), so an action that queries the model directly never triggers them — call self.check_object_permissions() yourself if you do. And do not wire an @action method up with .as_view(): that bypasses router setup and may ignore action settings including permission_classes, which is the usual cause of a permission that appears to be attached but never runs.
reference_contexts: If you have ad-hoc methods that should be routable, you can mark them as such with the @action decorator. Like regular actions, extra actions may be intended for either a single object, or an entire collection. To indicate this, set the detail argument to True or False. The router will configure its URL patterns accordingly.

By default, the URL pattern is based on the method name, and the URL name is the combination of the ViewSet.basename and the hyphenated method name. If you don't want to use the defaults for either of these values, you can instead provide the url_path and url_name arguments to the @action decorator.
@action(detail=True, methods=['post'], permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf]) def set_password(self, request, pk=None): ...
Do not use .as_view() with @action methods. It bypasses router setup and may ignore action settings like permission_classes. Use DefaultRouter for actions.
llm_response:
These are two separate knobs.

### URL Routing and `NoReverseMatch`
By default, the URL name is the combination of the `ViewSet.basename` and the hyphenated method name. When you change the URL segment using the `url_path` argument in the `@action` decorator, the URL name does not automatically update to match the new path. If your serializer is attempting to reverse the URL using the new path name, it will fail.

To fix the `NoReverseMatch` error, you must explicitly provide the `url_name` argument to the `@action` decorator to match the name your serializer expects:

```python
@action(detail=True, url_path='hyphenated-path', url_name='hyphenated-name')
def my_action(self, request, pk=None):
    ...
```

When reversing URLs for actions, it is recommended to use the `.reverse_action()` method, which prepends the `basename` automatically:
`self.reverse_action("hyphenated-name", args=[pk])`

### Permissions
The `permission_classes` argument in the `@action` decorator is the knob used to control access to the action. 

Regarding your issue with object-level permissions:
*   The `permission_classes` defined on the `@action` are consulted during dispatch.
*   If you are using object-level permissions, ensure your viewset logic correctly handles the object retrieval. The documentation notes that `get_*()` methods (such as `get_permissions()`) have access to the current view and can return different instances based on the action. You can inspect the `self.action` attribute on the viewset to adjust behavior dynamically if needed.

# Tutorial 6: ViewSets & Routers¶ {#tutorial-6-viewsets-routers}

REST framework includes an abstraction for dealing with
`ViewSets`
, that allows the developer to concentrate on modeling the state and interactions of the API, and leave the URL construction to be handled automatically, based on common conventions.

`ViewSet`
classes are almost the same thing as
`View`
classes, except that they provide operations such as
`retrieve`
, or
`update`
, and not method handlers such as
`get`
or
`put`
.

A
`ViewSet`
class is only bound to a set of method handlers at the last moment, when it is instantiated into a set of views, typically by using a
`Router`
class which handles the complexities of defining the URL conf for you.

llm_response:
By default, `ModelSerializer` does not automatically create or update nested related instances. When you use a nested serializer, you must explicitly override the `.create()` method in your `UserSerializer` to handle the creation of the related `Profile` instance.

As shown in the example for custom creation logic [5], you need to define a `create` method on your serializer:

```python
def create(self, validated_data):
    profile_data = validated_data.pop('profile')
    user = User.objects.create(**validated_data)
    Profile.objects.create(user=user, **profile_data)
    return user
```

Without this explicit logic, the `ModelSerializer` ignores the nested data during the save process, which explains why the `User` is created but the `Profile` is not.

### UpdateModelMixin¶ {#updatemodelmixin}

Provides a
`.update(request, *args, **kwargs)`
method, that implements updating and saving an existing model instance.

Also provides a
`.partial_update(request, *args, **kwargs)`
method, which is similar to the
`update`
method, except that all fields for the update will be optional.  This allows support for HTTP
`PATCH`
requests.

If an object is updated this returns a
`200 OK`
response, with a serialized representation of the object as the body of the response.

If the request data provided for updating the object was invalid, a
`400 Bad Request`
response will be returned, with the error details as the body of the response.

### DestroyModelMixin¶ {#destroymodelmixin}

Provides a
`.destroy(request, *args, **kwargs)`
method, that implements deletion of an existing model instance.

If an object is deleted this returns a
`204 No Content`
response, otherwise it will return a
`404 Not Found`
.

## API Reference¶ {#api-reference}

### AllowAny¶ {#allowany}

The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated
.

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

### IsAuthenticated¶ {#isauthenticated}

The
`IsAuthenticated`
permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

### IsAdminUser¶ {#isadminuser}

llm_response:
The reason your permission works on the detail endpoint but not the list endpoint is that object-level permissions (such as `IsOwner`) are only applied to retrieve, modify, and deletion actions [5]. For list actions, permission checks are applied to the entire object type rather than individual instances [5].

To scope a list response, you must use the `queryset` or `get_queryset()` method. The `queryset` attribute limits the general visibility of objects from the database, determining which objects will be listed [5].

To implement this, override the `get_queryset()` method in your view to filter the results based on the current user:

```python
def get_queryset(self):
    return Purchase.objects.filter(owner=self.request.user)
```

This ensures that the list endpoint only returns objects belonging to the authenticated user, as the `queryset` limits which objects are listed [5].

To fix the issue where your mobile client receives relative URLs instead of fully qualified URLs, you must include the current `request` in the serializer context when instantiating the `HyperlinkedModelSerializer`.

In your `views.py`, update the serializer instantiation as follows:

```python
serializer = AccountSerializer(accounts, many=True, context={'request': request})
```

### Why this happens
When using `HyperlinkedModelSerializer`, the serializer requires the `request` object to determine the appropriate hostname for generating fully qualified URLs (e.g., `http://api.example.com/accounts/1/`). Without it, the serializer defaults to relative URLs (e.g., `/accounts/1/`).

### Regarding the `ListAPIView`
The reason your colleague's `ListAPIView` works without extra code is that generic views provided by REST framework automatically include the `request` in the serializer context. Your current implementation using `APIView` does not do this automatically, which is why you must pass it explicitly. Providing the `request` context will also resolve the assertion errors you are encountering, as the serializer requires this context to correctly build the hyperlinked fields.

To accept a raw file upload via `PUT` without form encoding, you must use the `FileUploadParser`.

### 1. Update your view
You need to set the `parser_classes` attribute on your view to `FileUploadParser`. When using this parser, the file is accessed via the `'file'` key in `request.data`.

```python
from rest_framework.parsers import FileUploadParser
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class UploadView(APIView):
    parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]

    def put(self, request, filename, format=None):
        file_obj = request.data['file']
        # ... handle the file_obj ...
        return Response(status=204)
```

### 2. Handling the filename
The filename is captured from the URL path via the `filename` argument in the `put` method. Your existing URL configuration already supports this:

```python
# urls.py
path('upload/<str:filename>/', UploadView.as_view())
```

### 3. Client request
When using `FileUploadParser`, the file content is expected in the request body. You should ensure your client sends the request to the URL containing the filename, for example:

`curl -X PUT --data-binary @photo.jpg http://localhost:8000/upload/photo.jpg/`

The `415 Unsupported Media Type` error occurs because the default parsers (`multipart` and `json`) do not support raw binary uploads. Setting `parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]` allows the view to process the stream directly.

## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

In some circumstances instead of returning
`None`
, you may want to raise an
`AuthenticationFailed`
exception from the
`.authenticate()`
method.

Typically the approach you should take is:

If authentication is not attempted, return
`None`
.  Any other authentication schemes also in use will still be checked.
If authentication is attempted but fails, raise an
`AuthenticationFailed`
exception.  An error response will be returned immediately, regardless of any permissions checks, and without checking any other authentication schemes.

You
may
also override the
`.authenticate_header(self, request)`
method.  If implemented, it should return a string that will be used as the value of the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header in a
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response.

If the
`.authenticate_header()`
method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will return
`HTTP 403 Forbidden`
responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`

## Object level permissions¶ {#object-level-permissions}

REST framework permissions also support object-level permissioning.  Object level permissions are used to determine if a user should be allowed to act on a particular object, which will typically be a model instance.

### AuthenticationFailed¶ {#authenticationfailed}

Signature:
`AuthenticationFailed(detail=None, code=None)`

Raised when an incoming request includes incorrect authentication.

By default this exception results in a response with the HTTP status code "401 Unauthenticated", but it may also result in a "403 Forbidden" response, depending on the authentication scheme in use.  See the
authentication documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
for more details.

### NotAuthenticated¶ {#notauthenticated}

Signature:
`NotAuthenticated(detail=None, code=None)`

Raised when an unauthenticated request fails the permission checks.

By default this exception results in a response with the HTTP status code "401 Unauthenticated", but it may also result in a "403 Forbidden" response, depending on the authentication scheme in use.  See the
authentication documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
for more details.

If the
`.authenticate_header()`
method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will return
`HTTP 403 Forbidden`
responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

Note
When your custom authenticator is invoked by the request object's
`.user`
or
`.auth`
properties, you may see an
`AttributeError`
re-raised as a
`WrappedAttributeError`
. This is necessary to prevent the original exception from being suppressed by the outer property access. Python will not recognize that the
`AttributeError`
originates from your custom authenticator and will instead assume that the request object does not have a
`.user`
or
`.auth`
property. These errors should be fixed or otherwise handled by your authenticator.

llm_response:
To catch the uniqueness constraint before it reaches the database, you should use a `UniqueValidator` on the field in your serializer.

As shown in the documentation, uniqueness constraints are enforced by adding a `UniqueValidator` to the field's `validators` argument, passing the model's queryset to it:

```python
from rest_framework.validators import UniqueValidator

class BlogPostSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    slug = serializers.SlugField(
        max_length=100,
        validators=[UniqueValidator(queryset=BlogPost.objects.all())]
    )
    title = serializers.CharField(max_length=200)
```

This ensures the serializer validates the uniqueness of the field during `is_valid()`, preventing the database `IntegrityError` from occurring during the save process.

An arbitrary column is accepted because, when the `ordering_fields` attribute is not specified on the view, the `OrderingFilter` class defaults to allowing ordering on any readable field present on the serializer.

### ScopedRateThrottle¶ {#scopedratethrottle}

The
`ScopedRateThrottle`
class can be used to restrict access to specific parts of the API.  This throttle will only be applied if the view that is being accessed includes a
`.throttle_scope`
property.  The unique throttle key will then be formed by concatenating the "scope" of the request with the unique user id or IP address.

The allowed request rate is determined by the
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
setting using a key from the request "scope".

For example, given the following views...


`classContactListView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classContactDetailView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classUploadView(APIView):throttle_scope='uploads'...`


...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`

...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`


User requests to either
`ContactListView`
or
`ContactDetailView`
would be restricted to a total of 1000 requests per-day.  User requests to
`UploadView`
would be restricted to 20 requests per day.

The `@api_view` decorator defaults to accepting only `GET` requests. Any other method, including `POST`, will result in a "405 Method Not Allowed" response.

To allow `POST` requests, you must explicitly specify the allowed methods in the decorator:

```python
@api_view(['GET', 'POST'])
def create_thing(request):
    ...
```

Function-based views using `@api_view` require you to define the allowed methods manually.
